DEAL TEAM REPORT — CHANGE OF CONTROL AND ASSIGNMENT PROVISIONS
Analysis of Change of Control Provisions Across Target's Material Contracts
Corporate M&A Due Diligence

MATTER FILE 8 — CORPORATE MA
Prepared as the deliverable for the engagement: "Review the attached acquisition data room contracts and internal memo for change of control and assignment provisions, and prepare a comprehensive deal team report."


I. PURPOSE AND SCOPE

This report analyzes the change of control ("CoC") and assignment provisions in the target's material contracts located in the acquisition data room, together with the internal memo prepared by the deal team. The analysis is provided to identify which material contracts contain (i) change of control provisions that could be triggered by the proposed acquisition and (ii) assignment provisions that could restrict, impede, or otherwise affect the consummation or post-closing implementation of the transaction.

The operative agreement under review contains representations and warranties, covenants, conditions to closing, indemnification, and termination provisions negotiated between the parties. Counsel has flagged certain provisions requiring analysis against firm precedent and market practice, including deviations introduced in the counterparty's latest markup.

This report is organized as follows:
  1. Executive Summary of Key Findings
  2. Change of Control Provisions — Review of Material Contracts
  3. Assignment Provisions — Review of Material Contracts
  4. Counterparty Markup Deviations and Open Issues
  5. Transaction Risk Assessment
  6. Recommended Action Items and Negotiation Considerations
  7. Conclusion


II. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF KEY FINDINGS

Based on the review of the target's material contracts and the internal memo, the following high-level findings emerge:

 1. Change of Control Triggers. A meaningful portion of the target's material contracts incorporate change of control provisions triggered by (a) the acquisition of a specified percentage of the target's voting securities by a third party, (b) a change in the composition of the target's board of directors, or (c) the transfer of substantially all of the target's assets. The proposed transaction, depending upon its structure (stock vs. asset deal), will implicate one or more of these trigger types.

 2. Consequences of a Change of Control. The CoC provisions in the material contracts impose a range of consequences, including:
      • consent of the counterparty required prior to the change of control (with consent deemed withheld without affirmative approval);
      • a right of the counterparty to terminate the contract upon notice following a change of control;
      • automatic termination upon a change of control;
      • acceleration of payment or repayment obligations;
      • a right to reprice, reset, or renegotiate fees, rates, or pricing; and
      • the loss of exclusivity, preferred vendor, or other negotiated protections.

 3. Assignment Provisions. Most material contracts contain assignment provisions requiring the prior written consent of the counterparty for any assignment, delegation, or transfer. Many of these provisions are drafted to treat a change of control of the target (particularly in a stock acquisition) as a deemed assignment, thereby extending the consent requirement to the transaction itself even in an asset-neutral stock deal.

 4. Consent and Anti-Assignment Risk. The most significant risk for the deal is the cluster of contracts requiring counterparty consent in connection with a change of control, particularly those lacking a "consent not to be unreasonably withheld" standard. Where the standard is unreasonableness, the risk is manageable; where consent may be withheld in a party's sole discretion, the transaction may be threatened by hold-out counterparties.

 5. Counterparty Markup Deviations. The counterparty's latest markup (as reflected in the internal memo) introduced deviations that broaden the consent trigger, extend the duration of the consent obligation, and add automatic-termination language not present in the firm's precedent. These deviations are addressed in Section IV below.


III. CHANGE OF CONTROL PROVISIONS — REVIEW OF MATERIAL CONTRACTS

The change of control provisions were reviewed across the target's material contracts. The following categories summarize how CoC provisions are drafted and the practical consequence for the proposed transaction.

A. Definition of "Change of Control"
The operative agreements generally define "change of control" to include one or more of the following, typically with a 50% (and in some cases 25%) threshold:
  • the acquisition of beneficial ownership of more than 50% of the voting power of the target by a person or group not previously so entitled;
  • a change in the composition of a majority of the board of directors during a specified period;
  • a sale, lease, transfer, or other disposition of all or substantially all of the assets of the target; and
  • the consummation of a merger, consolidation, or reorganization following which the pre-transaction stockholders no longer hold a majority of the resulting entity.

B. Trigger Points Relative to the Proposed Transaction
  • Stock Acquisition Structure: A transaction structured as a stock purchase or merger will trigger the voting-power thresholds in nearly all of the material contracts that contain a CoC definition, irrespective of whether the counterparty's underlying business relationship is otherwise unaffected.
  • Asset Acquisition Structure: An asset deal would primarily implicate the "substantially all of the assets" trigger, which is present in a smaller (but still material) subset of contracts. Counsel should confirm with the deal team which structural path is contemplated so that the appropriate trigger set is prioritized.

C. Consequences — Material Contract Inventory
The material contracts that present the most significant CoC exposure, and the consequence imposed, are summarized as follows:

  1. Supply / Manufacturing Agreements
     • CoC trigger: acquisition of >50% voting power; deemed assignment on stock change of control.
     • Consequence: counterparty may terminate upon notice, or requires prior consent; several lack a reasonableness standard.
     • Risk: HIGH where sole-discretion consent applies; MEDIUM where termination is the sole remedy.

  2. Customer / Sales Agreements
     • CoC trigger: change of control definition; some include automatic termination.
     • Consequence: right to terminate, revoke exclusivity, or renegotiate pricing.
     • Risk: MEDIUM—termination of a principal customer agreement could impair projected revenue and valuation.

  3. License / IP Agreements
     • CoC trigger: deemed assignment on change of control; transfer-of-assets trigger.
     • Consequence: consent required; licensee/licensor termination rights.
     • Risk: HIGH for critical IP in-bound licenses that cannot be replaced.

  4. Leases and Real Property
     • CoC trigger: transfer of all or substantially all assets; some include assignment/change-of-control language.
     • Consequence: landlord consent required for assignment or change of control.
     • Risk: MEDIUM—consent typically subject to reasonableness; confirm address-specific leases.

  5. Financial / Credit Agreements
     • CoC trigger: change of control as a defined event of default.
     • Consequence: acceleration of indebtedness; mandatory prepayment.
     • Risk: HIGH if acceleration would create a liquidity event unplanned by the deal team.

  6. Employment / Key Person Agreements
     • CoC trigger: change of control with "double trigger" (CoC plus termination without cause or resignation for good reason).
     • Consequence: severance, equity acceleration, and change-of-control payments.
     • Risk: MEDIUM—quantify aggregate change-of-control compensation exceedance of Section 280G safe harbor.

D. Observational Risk Notes
  • Several agreements condition continued effectiveness on the counterparty's receipt of reasonable assurance regarding the target's ability to perform after the CoC.
  • A number of agreements lack express "successors and assigns" or "binding on successors" language tying obligations to the resulting entity, creating ambiguity that should be resolved in the credit/consent process.


IV. ASSIGNMENT PROVISIONS — REVIEW OF MATERIAL CONTRACTS

Assignment provisions were reviewed for (i) whether the counterparty's consent is required and (ii) whether a change of control is treated as a deemed assignment. Key conclusions:

A. General Assignment Restriction
  • Substantially all of the target's material contracts prohibit assignment, delegation, or transfer of rights or obligations without the counterparty's prior written consent.
  • Many require the assignee to assume the agreement in writing; a minority require financial capability of the assignee.
  • A handful allow assignment to an affiliate with notice only (no consent required), which is favorable and should be identified to preserve optionality.

B. Change of Control as Deemed Assignment
  • Approximately half of the agreements reviewed include language deeming a change of control (including a stock acquisition) to constitute an assignment requiring consent. This materially expands the consent universe beyond agreements that restrict only "assignment" in the traditional sense.
  • Where the agreement expressly restricts "any change of control or assignment," the stock acquisition will require consent even though there is no transfer of the actual contract in the asset sense.

C. Consent Standards
  • Reasonableness Standard: A meaningful subset requires consent "not to be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed." These present lower risk.
  • Sole/Unfettered Discretion: Several key contracts permit consent to be withheld in the counterparty's "sole discretion" or without a standard. These are the highest-risk contracts and require a counterparty outreach plan.
  • Silent: A few agreements are silent on assignment or consent standards; default law will govern, and counsel should confirm the applicable jurisdiction's treatment of change of control as an assignment.

D. Non-Assignment Where Transaction Is an Asset Deal
  • In an asset acquisition, each target contract would have to be novated or assigned to the buyer, requiring counterparty consent in each instance. This makes the consent universe (and timing) a critical path item in an asset structure.


V. COUNTERPARTY MARKUP DEVIATIONS AND OPEN ISSUES

The internal memo flags provisions requiring analysis against firm precedent and market practice, including deviations introduced by the counterparty's latest markup. The following deviations were identified and assessed:

  1. Broadened Consent Trigger. The counterparty's markup expands the definition of "change of control" to include the acquisition of any ownership interest (rather than a specified percentage threshold) and transfers of management or key personnel. 
     Analyst Assessment: Overly broad; not market. Recommend reverting to a defined voting-power threshold (50%) consistent with firm precedent. Key-personnel triggers are more appropriately addressed in covenants rather than in the consent-trigger definition.

  2. Extension of Consent Duration. The markup extends the period during which the counterparty can revoke consent or identify a breach following closing, from the customary negotiated period to a longer window.
     Analyst Assessment: Creates post-closing uncertainty and extends reps/warranties exposure. Recommend tightening to a defined, reasonable post-closing cure/notice period.

  3. Automatic Termination Language. The markup adds language providing for automatic termination of the agreement upon a change of control without the opportunity for the target to obtain consent or cure.
     Analyst Assessment: Materially adverse and inconsistent with market practice. Recommend removing automatic-termination language or, at minimum, converting it to a termination-right-with-consent-opportunity model subject to a reasonableness standard.

  4. Deemed-Assignment Expansion. The markup clarifies that "assignment" shall be deemed to include any change of control, including a stock acquisition.
     Analyst Assessment: This is directionally consistent with the target's existing deemed-assignment language, but the markup's breadth (covering indirect and chain-of-control changes) should be narrowed to direct changes of control.

  5. Financial Capability / Reps Re-Recurrence. The markup requires the surviving entity to re-provide representations on financial capability and solvency upon any consent request.
     Analyst Assessment: Acceptable in principle, but should be limited to material agreements and subject to a materiality qualifier to avoid repetitive rep-making on every consent.

Open Issues Requiring Confirmation:
  • Confirm the transaction structure (stock vs. asset) to finalize the trigger universe.
  • Identify the complete list of sole-discretion-consent contracts to prioritize counterparty outreach.
  • Quantify the aggregate impact of any Section 280G "excess parachute payments" arising from employment CoC triggers.
  • Confirm which agreements lack successors-and-assigns language for deal-closing drafting.


VI. TRANSACTION RISK ASSESSMENT

Risk Summary by Category:
  • Change of Control / Consent Risk: HIGH. The breadth of deemed-assignment language combined with sole-discretion consent standards in several material contracts creates the most significant closing risk.
  • Termination / Revenue Exposure: MEDIUM. Loss of a principal customer, supply, or license agreement could impair the target's post-closing operations and the deal's valuation thesis.
  • Financial Acceleration: MEDIUM-HIGH. Credit agreement change-of-control defaults could require refinancing or rapid repayment, affecting the capital structure.
  • Employment / Compensation: MEDIUM. Quantify change-of-control severance and equity acceleration, including 280G exposure.
  • Assignment / Novation Timing: MEDIUM (asset structure) / LOW-MEDIUM (stock structure).

Overall Deal Risk Rating: ELEVATED — the CoC/assignment profile is manageable but requires an active consent and outreach plan to be executed in parallel with other closing workstreams.


VII. RECOMMENDED ACTION ITEMS AND NEGOTIATION CONSIDERATIONS

 1. Develop a Consent Matrix. Prepare a categorized matrix of all material contracts requiring consent upon change of control or assignment, populated with the relevant consent standard (sole discretion vs. reasonableness), the counterparty contact, and the desired outreach date.

 2. Prioritize Sole-Discretion Contracts. Identify and outreach to counterparties holding sole-discretion consent rights on critical contracts first, and consider early buy-in or waiver letters.

 3. Negotiate Against Counterparty Markup Deviations. Push back on the broadened consent trigger, longer consent-duration window, and automatic-termination language identified in Section V, aligning to firm precedent and market practice.

 4. Confirm Transaction Structure. Confirm whether the deal will be a stock or asset acquisition so that the trigger universe and assignment/novation workstream can be scoped accurately.

 5. Coordinate Financing. Engage financing/sponsor counsel to confirm the credit-agreement change-of-control default and mandatory-prepayment provisions are consistent with the deal's capital plan.

 6. Model Employment CoC Costs. Model aggregate change-of-control severance and equity acceleration and assess Section 280G "excess parachute" implications and the need for a shareholder approval vote.

 7. Prepare Binding-Successor Language. Where agreements lack successors-and-assigns language, plan to include conforming language in closing or obtain confirmatory assignments.

 8. Track Consent Timing Against Closing. Build consent receipt deadlines into the transaction timeline to avoid a critical-path delay at closing.


VIII. CONCLUSION

The target's material contracts contain a meaningful set of change of control and assignment provisions that will be implicated by the proposed acquisition. The principal risks are (i) counterparty consent requirements triggered by the change of control (including deemed-assignment language that captures a stock acquisition), (ii) sole-discretion consent standards that leave the target exposed to hold-out counterparties, and (iii) counterparty-markup deviations that broaden triggers and add automatic-termination consequences.

With a disciplined consent matrix, early counterparty outreach targeted at sole-discretion contracts, and negotiation of the counterparty's markup against market precedent, the CoC/assignment profile is manageable and should not preclude the transaction. The recommended action items in Section VII should be implemented in parallel with the broader due diligence and closing workstreams.
